name: Beard dye

lead: Beard dye is a temporary or semi-permanent coloring product for facial hair, used to cover gray hairs or even out patchy color. Types include quick-wash gels, brush-on formulas and dye-free fillers.
Users report that it can make a beard look denser and younger. Most permanent-style products contain aromatic amine dyes such as PPD, which is the main safety issue.

paras: Oxidative dyes penetrate the hair shaft and react to form color in the cortex, while temporary dyes only coat the surface. Choosing a shade slightly lighter than the natural color is commonly described as looking more natural.

Hair-dye allergy to para-phenylenediamine is common and can be serious. Dermatology reviews recommend patch testing, avoiding use on irritated skin and care near the eyes. Cross-reactions with related dyes are frequent. The coloring effect is reported as reliable but requires regular touch-ups.

lead: Beard dye is a temporary, semi-permanent or permanent coloring product for facial hair, used to cover gray hairs or even out patchy color. Types include quick-wash gels, brush-on formulas and dye-free fillers.

Hair coloring generally falls into permanent, demi-permanent, semi-permanent and temporary categories; temporary pigments coat the hair surface and wash out, while permanent products use oxidation chemistry.[1] The main safety issue is allergy to para-phenylenediamine (PPD), a common ingredient in permanent dyes.[2][3] A Mayo Clinic series reported beard dermatitis from PPD in Arab men who dye their beards.[4]
infobox: Days to weeks; touch-ups as hair grows
None found for beard dye specifically

paras: Per Wikipedia, permanent color usually contains ammonia and is mixed with a developer to change color permanently, while temporary color only adheres to the surface and shampoos out.[1] Roots are typically retouched every 4 to 6 weeks on scalp hair as regrowth appears.[1] Plant-based dyes such as henna and indigo have a long history of use.[1]
Wikipedia reports hair-dye recipes in Assyrian texts and the Egyptian Ebers Papyrus, and the 1856 discovery of mauveine by William Perkin as the start of the synthetic dye industry.[1]

Wikipedia lists skin irritation, allergy, hair breakage and unexpected color as reported effects and notes that the IARC has classed some hair-dye chemicals as mutagenic or carcinogenic in laboratory studies.[1] Manufacturers recommend a patch test; some European dermatologists advise against home patch testing because it can itself sensitize.[1] Reviews of PPD allergy describe contact dermatitis with frequent cross-reactions to related compounds.[2][3] A report of eight Arab men at the Mayo Clinic documented beard dermatitis linked to PPD dyes, an at-risk group because beards are commonly dyed.[4]
Beard coloring is discussed on general forums such as the Straight Dope Message Board.[5]
No trials of beard dye for appearance outcomes were found. Related clinical literature consists of case series and reviews of PPD contact allergy, including beard dermatitis.[2][3][4]

timeline.event: William Perkin discovers mauveine, the first synthetic dye.[1]
